rv.q: But by the time the superb ensemble start singing staunch activist Billy Bragg's 'The Company', a warning against giving in to the bad guys, don't be surprised if you want to change the world.
It is — allegedly — an evening of political satire, but it’s one that entirely lacks the biting wit and trenchancy of the best examples of the genre, such as Yes, Minister and The Thick Of It.
So it's all the sadder to report that the venture is a bit disappointing and underpowered – a sequence of pot shots at fairly obvious targets.
This revue is a bit of a mishmash, as mixed-up as your average mojito.
But however well-intentioned, the evening lacks topical bite.
A company of six actors shows great versatility and energy in delivering 1¾ hours of sometimes chilling satire written by a sparkling selection of playwrights.

All in all, this is a fun but thought-provoking piece of theatre, likely to infuriate and entertain in equal measure, and Out Of Joint is to be congratulated on bringing to a West End stage the political Britain we live in right now.
Unfortunately for a large portion of A View from Islington North, phasers are set firmly to stun.
While Hare’s piece is by far the most intelligent and well-imagined, the others feel as if they are squatting a bit too complacently on familiar ground.

cn.t: Mixed reception for this political satire anthology featuring top UK playwrights. Critics find the sketches uneven and often obvious in their targets, though some praise its punchy, unapologetically left-wing energy and strong performances.
